review: It's cool, and well worth the price.

Dark Fear is basically what you'd get if a Sierra adventure game from the 90s got possessed by a demon, and combining its atmospheric horror/adventure with RPG elements together nicely to tell a compelling, yet grizzly tale. Simply booting the game and seeing the floppy disk boot screen alone had me smiling. But you know what else this game reminds me of? Cabin in the Woods.

Anyway, combat is fairly simple. There's a little power meter you time your hits with, and it's quite satisfying once you get used to it. The score counter at the top (old school Sierra style) hits different when it ticks up after you solve something. RPG elements sneak in too, like leveling and buying gears or hunting for animals and fishing, which I wasn't expecting but totally welcomed.

Now, some warning: pixel hunting is real here. I spent an embarrassing amount of time looking for a rock. A rock. The environments aren't huge, but some items are basically camouflaged into the scenery. There's also a trick where dragging an item around lights things up, which helps, but it's somewhat clunky.

Still, none of that stopped me from being completely hooked on the mystery. Its flaws are small compared to the quality and mystery of the overall experience. Honestly a shame it sat untouched in my library since I picked it up back in Oct 2016 — but that's on me.

영국산 호러 어드벤처 RPG 게임.

RPG 파트는 사냥, 낚시를 통해서 동물의 가죽, 생선 등을 팔아서 돈을 벌고 재료로 사용해서 무기/방어구를 업그레이드하고. 몬스터와 싸우는 전투 모드가 있는데. 그런 개념이 있는 것 자체는 괜찮지만, 미니 게임이 단순 노가다라 지루하다. 전투는 딱 정해진 것만 나오지만. 후반부의 파워 인플레이션을 따라가려면 장비 업그레이드가 필수라 파밍 노가다가 강제된다.

어드벤처 파트는 80년대 시에라표 어드벤처를 구현하고 있어 스코어(점수) 시스템제로 운영되는데, 퍼즐 난이도는 쉬운 편이고, 월드 맵에서 아이콘을 클릭해 장소 이동을 한 번에 하고, 장소 내에서의 이동도 갈 수 있는 장소가 딱딱 정해져 있어  길 찾기도 어렵지 않아서 쾌적하다.

스토리는 전반부는 농가에 홀로 있는 소녀 악령과 싸우고, 섬에 있는 폐가에 숨겨진 비밀을 파헤찰 때 호러물로서 흥미진진한데. 후반부로 넘어가면 거대 게, 고블린, 웨어울프, 사이클롭스 같은 판타지 크리쳐랑 싸우는 거 나오니 공포 분위기가 깨진다. 거기다 마지막 반전은 '나는 너의 XX'로 존나 식상한데. 이게 떡밥을 던지고 회수하는 과정에서의 극적 빌드 업을 거치지 않고, 갑자기 툭 튀어 나온 것이라 스토리의 완성도도 떨어진다.

전반부는 괜찮은데 후반부에 말아 먹은 케이스로, 판타지 성격을 버리고 호러물에 온전히 집중했다면 더 나은 결과물이 나오지 않았을까 싶다.

Although I'm not what one would call an 'avid' Horror fan, seeing as the genre itself is a finicky one to get right when it comes down to video games and the complex art of it's unique interactive medium that is gameplay, Dark Fear is certainly one such horror game that intrigued me enough that, even somewhat knowing what I was getting into as far as what to expect here, the homage to those old 16-bit AGI games that focused on the adventure point and click style of games that was one of the pioneers of the video game industry back in the mid-to-late 1980's is something admirable and, as a result, caused me to take a chance with this fun little indie.

Now, the big question that matters most here: Is it worth the asking price? As no doubt a game's worth is largely dependant on it's fun and what makes it stand out from the crowd as well as, to a lesser degree, it's replayability and overall length. Though the last point largely depends on what genre of game we're talking about here, something that makes Dark Fear quite the odd one at that!

For indeed, Dark Fear is labelled as a 'Horror RPG' of sorts, which is indeed true although I should emphasise here that the focus is more on the 'horror' aspect than it is the traditional 'Role Playing Game' part, since the atmosphere created through the viewpoint of this AGI-esque world reminiscent of the likes of ICOM Simulation's Uninvited and Déjà Vu is quite spooky, perhaps one might say even hair-raising to the point that it'll give your shoulders shudders and put you just a little on edge in some of the more horror-esque places of this game!

Although to touch upon the RPG aspects of this game, Dark Fear does indeed include combat with various monsters throughout the game and, as a result, has a variety of mechanics to bear in mind here, since starting off it's a matter of having a good melee weapon and sufficient armour alongside enough health potions but, later on, this gets expanded to a powerful ranged weapon that enables the use of various bolts to deal even higher damage alongside 'special' bolts that are usable after 2 regular attacks to exploit specific enemy weaknesses alongside magic tattoos that give you protection from the nasty special abilities of some enemies later on in the game!

In essence, dealing damage comes down to a simple matter of getting as close to the center as possible before clicking, with the closer you get the higher the 'strength' of your attack. Though this game's means of handling it's currency is a bit interesting, as not too much grinding is needed if you don't fail any battles and spend wisely, however this game's method of gaining gold through the use of hunting and fishing to capture various animals (the former for pelts for armour at a fair price whilst the latter is purely for gold and sell a little higher on average as a result) can be a tad tedious if you make multiple mistakes and have to grind for supplies again although, thankfully, dying will not have any permanent consequences or loss of progress outside of having to regain potions or ammo used.

Also, as far as the story of Dark Fear itself is concerned, it is definitely well-told and keeps you in suspense as you make your adventures across Diablo in increasingly higher stakes, add in the sudden spooky moment or even outright jump scare (Yes, 'Emily' did catch me off-guard even when knowing *that* dialogue meant something was going to happen, haven't had a good scare like that in a long time!) and it makes for quite the engrossing horror game to play and immerse yourself into, even with the RPG mechanics sometimes feeling like padding to make the game somewhat longer!

If I did have to give some criticism, there is a way to mute the music which, whilst great, is problematic with it's copyrighted material that ensures that any published videos on the big video platforming websites such as YouTube or Twitch will pose a problem for content creators and the likes. Also it is impossible to mute the sound in the game outside of just muting your PC, which I feel is a tad unusual as most games with basic settings tend to let you control the volume of the music and sounds or, at the very least, turn them on and off separately.

Overall though, I'd say Dark Fear is well-worth the price, even not being a fan of the genre itself for the most part, as I quite enjoyed it's dark story and the themes surrounding it's more disturbing elements alongside generally the gameplay being well-paced and not having any frustrating moments, save for a puzzle or two that took me a while to figure out the solution to!

TLDR Version:

• Excellent choice of graphics that helps to create a dark and foreboding world of many horrors that await the player with it's 16-bit AGI graphics from old point and click games (+)
• A scary story told rather well through both subtle elements of horror that put the player on edge as well as more obvious scare tactics when the moment calls for it without overuse or overstaying it's welcome (+)
• Gameplay balance between the horror and RPG moments is well-balanced for the most part, ensuring that the combat is easy to get into once money can be farmed through hunting and fishing methods (+)
• The game isn't too long that makes it feel like the gameplay is stretched out more than it should, nor is it too short that it feels like corners were clearly cut (+)
• Music used in this game is excellent for the overall mood of the game, be it the intense high-octane action when experiencing combat or the gloomy and sinister songs playing when in a haunted area (+)

• The grinding for money can be problematic for some, especially if they make mistakes that cost them plenty of supplies that requires more farming (-)
• There is little replayability once the game has been completed outside of reliving certain scary moments and potentially speedrunning it (-)
• 16-bit ACI graphics may prove to be off-putting for those looking for a more realistic horror game (-)
• Music is copyrighted and could prove to be an issue for content creators, with regards to copyright strikes, as well as sounds not being able to be muted (-)

Dark Fear takes inspiration from old adventure games, complete with a set score counter. The game is basically baby's first RPG with your path being very linear, but this isn't a bad thing. The charm of the game comes from trying to constantly improve your character while also looking forward to the next interesting setpieces.

Besides one time enemy encounters, you hunt and fish to make money, use the money to buy equipment to fight stronger enemies. That's the gameplay loop of Dark Fear. The process could have been pretty boring but the one thing that makes it so fun is that every new path you discover has something interesting. More often than not, the locations you visit has something horrible in it and it's fun to encounter those horrors. This game also has quite a bit of jumpscares and every single one of them works in my opinion. The game knows the importance of distracting you and while you're looking away, hits you with a jumpscare. It worked with me everytime.

The playtime is surprisingly long (took 4 hours in my case) and the price is pretty fair. Combined with 30+ achievements Dark Fear is a game that should definitely be tried by the lovers of horror / adventure - RPG genres.

[h1]SUMMARY[/h1]
I originally purchased this game thinking it would have an interesting Lovecraftian or Sam Rami-esque story and atmosphere and be more focused on adventure-game thematics and gameplay. Instead, most of the game is grinding, contrived writing, mixed with the most cliched horror tropes you can imagine. It almost felt borderline parody, what with one of your weapons for some reason being a katana that's described as "sharpest folded steel blade ever," enemies using typical "I'll crush you, you pathetic weakling" banter, and the writing seeming so rote and trite that it's hard to imagine this was made with any sort of passion.

The gameplay consists of you wandering around on the map, fast-travelling from point to point to solve puzzles and battle enemies using RPG mechanics. The problem is the RPG mechanics are incredibly bare-bones, you attack, eventually you get a crossbow that requires specific kinds of ammo, there's a special attack, there's a flat armor upgrade, there's healing potions, and then there's tattoos which are designed for specific enemies in mind so will only be used once or twice, like-wise with the special ammunition. Everything in the game is almost a flat upgrade, except for a couple enemies that require variation. Armor is a flat upgrade, weapon is a flat upgrade, ammunition for the most part is a flat upgrade, and the special ammo you use is only useful against very specific enemies you encounter so unless you're reading a walkthrough you'll be wasting money on the wrong ammo trying to figure out which ammo the enemy is weak against, then grinding to get more ammo. The hunting mechanic is the fast-reload mechanic from Gears of War, and you sit there clicking the mouse every couple of seconds to successfully catch them. It's a mind numbing grinding experience that requires neither effort, skill, or intelligence, it only requires patience. The puzzles vary between being excessively simple, so much so you almost think you're being tricked and then come to find out "Nope, that's actually how simple it is," and being so cryptic and hidden that you'll overlook the slightest detail which will cause you to desperately look through each location for the slightest thing that's clickable or interactable. In essence, its adventure mechanics are just as lazy as the RPG mechanics, but not as boring as the hunting mechanics. Speaking of the combat, there's no fear of death since you just respawn at the starting location without losing anything other than the equipment you used, requiring you to grind longer to get more money to buy back what you used up or different gear. The gameplay can be described quite simply as "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ annoying."

Now for the horror, oh boy the horror. Werewolves, bears, and demons, oh my! The game realizes that it's not actually scary or creepy and so it literally uses LOUD NOISES!!!!!!! with sudden imagery to jump-scare you into feeling any sense of dread. If this was done once or twice, I could live with it. It's done around 5 or 6 times. Jump scares need to be earned, throwing them at people randomly does nothing but piss them off. The sprite work is at least decent, although a few of the creatures look a little goofy and completely unintimidating, such as the Werewolf, Cyclops, and the Banshee. Even the Guardian himself is rather lackluster, going for a stereotypical hooved winged devil approach instead of something more sinister and original. Nope, the big bad at the end of the game is literally Satan from South Park.

The sound design is the only positive, with tracks that can be soothing or eerie, unfortunately they aren't matched by the environments and game design and the music comes off as being discordant with the rest of the atmosphere of the game. Whoever did the OST put in far more effort than anyone else on this project, if it was a team of individuals.

The story is yadda yadda yadda, wake up in random cabin, "oh no, why am I here," some guy lost his daughter who became possessed or corrupted or whatever, you help him, there's some rich types who became evil by practicing evil magic that need to be killed, "BAAHAHAHAHAHA, IT WAS ME, YOUR FATHER ALL ALONG!" Enough with it, the story is unoriginal, uninspired, and introduces several characters that go nowhere, as if having the time-wasting hunting grind segments wasn't enough, this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ time-vampire of a game then has you going to some "icy fortress" to meet this "ice queen" who exists for no other reason than to give you an excuse to fight some other random monster and collect a few token items to move the plot along. Who is she? Why is there some ice queen at the top of this mountain? Who cares? Not me!

The gameplay is boring and filled with grind, the story is generic, cliched, nonsense, the soundtrack is alright, the atmosphere is stereotypical at best, and the whole experience made me want to wish I could just take it all back and spend my time doing something of more value, like masturbating. But, since I can't, I'll offer this review as a warning that you should heed. Don't waste your time here. Buy From Beyond instead.

[h1]OVERALL SCORE[/h1]
Never Buy.

[h1]REPLAY VALUE[/h1]
Light.

The game isn't bad, I just don't really recommend it. It has charming graphics, nice music and a decent atmosphere. I didn't even know it was originally a mobile game, I just thought it was retro/minimalistic, so that is an achievement as well. It took only a few hours to finish, so it didn't overstay its welcome.

However, it just isn't very interesting or really engaging. The gameplay is barebones, though not painful, progress is pretty railroaded and there is a bit of grind, although not much. The horror elements are pretty standard and the few jumpscares are really basic. The story is pretty simple, though I found the ending funny. Overall not a terrible time, but I don't think I would have played it if I knew more about it.

I'm really on the fence how to rate this game. It starts charming and resembles an easy version fo the Cube Escape series first. New mechanics get introduced which blend well into the game. The balancing is top-notch: You can clearly see the math made to balance out weapons, armor, additional buffs with the next enemy's hp and damage. Even the no-brain busywork intersections you're forced to partake in to earn some money or find some ingredients are layed out right - they are chilled interruption of the gameplay at certain points and are never stretched out too far.
That might also give you an idea about the game's downside. It's extremely linear. The options you can chose from are not real options (more mandatory upgrades), and every fight is supposed to be taken one way, and will require the highest gear available at this point together with some items exploiting the next enemy's weakpoints.
The gameplay is rather shallow. There are some underdeveloped puzzle sections, but mostly it's a timing game - you've got to click at the right moment for full damage or to catch an animal, and that's it. Towards the end the combats become a bit more harder (read: longer, and you aren't allowed to miss your timings too often), but that's about it. I can image some ppl enjoy that kind of simplistic, somewhat lowbrow click-fest, but was bored from it after a while. It feels more like a casual handygame than anything. Have you ever played Hero of the Kingdom? Dispite being a tad more challenging, it felt more and more like that. At some point you just recognize the patterns/mechanics, and you grind through them. I wouldn't be suprised if it was made by the same ppl to be honest.
Last, but not least, the story is not worth it's name. It's as generic as the title of this game might suggest, stitching toghether all the horror trophes you've seend hundreds of times in a rather lame way full of logic loopholes. While the presentation and the atmosphere worked out, the story became so lame and anti-climatic that I was close to give up two fight before the game's end - the game had nothing to offer anymore ... no interesting mechanics, no interesting plot, no nothing. I wouldn't say it overstayed it's welcome after 6 hours, but the problem is that after 3, 4 hours you just realize you've seen all there is to see basically, and after that you just keep going because you enjoy the gameplay loop (I didn't) or because the progression bar promises you that you're almost done anyway (yeah, that's me).

The soundtrack is incredible, and absolutely elevates the game.

The writing is okay, and there's some actual wildness to the worldbuilding, but it gets blander towards the end than it is in the beginning.

There are genuine rpg elements and gamebook-style combat in Dark Fear, but they aren't developed fully, and they typically consist of "get the best available gear before you proceed." Getting that gear requires a weird, slow grind where you click a storm-stopper to endlessly harvest fish and animals.

The game's puzzles genuinely aren't bad. I'm puzzle-impaired, but I got through everything without consulting a guide. Solutions are pretty rational, and you're never completely overloaded with inventory items.

There *are* some really obnoxious jumpscares, but they're so obnoxious that for me they wrapped all the way back around and became super charming.

Overall, this definitely has some odd design choices, but I can't bring myself to fault it for them. I had a blast the whole time I was playing, and so I'm going to call Dark Fear a gem.

Drawing lots of inspiration from the old Sierra point-and-click adventure games, with a little dash of Oregon Trail and some basic old-school RPG mechanics, Dark Fear succeeds at crossing all three of these and adds a healthy dose of creepy atmosphere and some good scares.  I'm only about a quarter of the way through the game, but already I can tell that it's only going to get even better from here.  Although the music doesn't match the retro art style, it definitely helps up the creep factor.  For example, the music in the old plantation house creates a great sense of forboding, and that's on top of the unsettling pixel art.

The story so far is very light and not too full of bloaty lore and backstory.  You're an amnesiac who wakes up in a old cabin surrounded by a forest filled with nightmarish creatures.  You've got to figure out who you are and how you got there, all while solving some puzzles and helping the folks in the nearby village.  There's demons, dark magicians, forest beasts, and other unspeakable horrors... and fishing minigames!  Yes, you can hunt and fish to sell to the villagers for extra gold.

Overall, considering the low price point of this game, even if it's only a few hours long, it's a spooky good time and a fun nostalgic trip.  The puzzles aren't too difficult for players familiar with this type of game, and the RPG elements aren't deep enough to become complicated.  It's just right.

EDIT: After an additional 10 hours of playing, my original review still stands, although I do have to add a caveat for achievement hunters - in order to complete the game, you actually HAVE to get all of the achievements in one run.  So if you missed one, and there are a few that are easily missable, you will most likely have to play through again.  And the final achievement is for getting all of the achievements in-game, not just getting them in Steam.  So yeah, PERFECT RUN.
If you have any love at all for classic adventure games (especially 80s-to-mid-90s macintosh adventure games), horror games, or fantasy games, I recommend you play the crap out of this.

Dark Fear, a horror point and click adventure with some slight RPG elements, and hunting/fishing minigames that are integrated in the plot. The controls are very simple because it was originally a smartphone game, but there's no problem in controlling it with the mouse.
The game imitates DOS-era adventures and especially Sierra ones (but not nearly as cruel), even having a mock DOS booting screen. The atmosphere of mountain horror folklore is good, the jump scares are few (and thanks for that since everyone goes overboard with them) but effective and well-integrated, the tale of dark magic compelling and with a couple disturbing moments, the puzzles are simple without being insulting, the graphics quite nice in their clean pixelated glory, the final twist is neat and everything in general simply works. 
Only thing I disliked was the super-cheesy final battle, a stereotypical giant devil with a rock BGM, kind of strange since the rest of the soundtrack is very good and atmospheric. Good job for the developers (who are British and not Americans despite the game's setting) for having far exceeded my expectations and making a near-perfect imitation of 80s-early 90s point and click games.

Dark Fear surprised me when I played through it as mobile games don't often translate well to a big bulky desktop.  That feeling that the game is too tiny and bare bones can often overtake qualities that were more apparent on a handheld device.  This one is somehow different.  Perhaps it's the amalgamation of styles and their successful combination that gives Dark Fear its legs. 

The experience could have been much longer (ignore my playtime as I distinctly remember having to pause this one for a very long, long time...hey, sometimes you have to pee for 3 or 4 hours or whatever I was doing) and sometimes you'll be wishing that the systems at work were even more complexly engaging (the battles have only a small but efficient set of commands) but for all of that this was an entertaining experience.  

The ol' "wake up at an abandoned log cabin" horror trope starts this one off but soon you are clicking from point to point on an overworld map and getting down n' dirty after leaving the first screen to see what haunted ruin awaits thee.  I say leave the first screen because Dark Fear balances its time between point n' click adventuring where you need to find necessary items to further progress and unlock new area, earning enough cash to buy better gear to defeat your enemies in turn based RPG battles and thusly getting back to exploring some dark, indoor/outdoor areas where jumpscares and other jolts can happen in your quest for key artifacts of progression.

If it sounds weird in description and it is; that's because the game occupies a quirky niche between genre realms.  Yes, Dark Fear is part Dragon Warrior I, part OG Alone in the Darks, part King's Quest and quite good in terms of overall execution...especially for a smallscreen gem.  It'll suck you into its fairly brief runtime (it took me about 5 hours to complete) and just when you think you're about to put it down and play something else...you don't.  Well, I didn't anyway.  In some ways it rams together a variety of unique styles and comes up with something that's a lot of fun but could use slightly more depth in each department if there is ever a sequel or a follow-up.  Still, it shocked me in that you couldn't simply bumble one command to win a battle with your eyes closed and that required some pinch of wits to know what to use where.  There are no infuriating pixel hunts but the game is involved enough to keep your eyes peeled and your brown bent, while being relaxing to the point that this is a good game to sink into after midnight when a long day of work is done.

In terms of flavor it reminds me a lot of Cloak and Dagger's excellent The Legend of Hand.  Though the two games utilize entirely opposite settings/scenarios they both possess that same "throw everything at the wall and see what sticks" approach to what are largely twists on classic adventure titles.  It's this aesthetic that gives Dark Fear its juice.  

The plot isn't fantastic but it's the gameplay that pushes you to further unravel it.  I was always satisfied when I would see that I've unlocked new areas and wondered what problem I might encounter next; a boss monster that wouldn't go down with a hearty exhale, a decaying abode to explore, a puzzle to solve, items that need brought to a new location to unlock another set piece and much, much more.  This was a solid and eerie cult gem that engages the player on a slightly higher level than drifting off to some of the lesser endless walking sims out there whenever the mind isn't up for a more white-knuckle gaming evening.  

Cool stuff, I'd love to see a sequel built from the ground up for us desktop/laptop commandos out there.

Rough around the edges, but worth a look at its cheap price.

You wake up in a dark cabin in the middle of the woods with the classic gaming trope, amnesia. You don't know who you are and your only clue to what's going on is a picture of a man hanging on the wall. It soon becomes apparent that something bad has happened in this world. Demons run amok, and once happy locations are now the homes of vicious monsters.

The presentation is top notch, with fantastic pixel art and a moody score that really sells a feeling of unease and suspense. Something as simple as a house off in the distance is foreboding and creepy.

As for the game itself, it's a hybrid of point and click adventure games with turn based combat. The puzzles in each area are just clever enough to be fun to solve, but aren't too taxing. The combat is extremely simple. Attacking is always the go to action, no spells or nothing. The only wrinkle is a bar that moves back and forth along the bottom. Click at the right time and you will do maximum possible damage. Click outside the middle and you might do 75% damage ormiss altogether. It works in the beginning of the game.

The aforementioned rough edges come into play as the game goes on. You can use money acquired from battles to purchase new weapons, armor, and healing, as well as a few other things. Because the battling is so simple, and every single battle is scripted, each one is designed with a very specific course of action in mind, and upgrading armor, which gives you more health, is an absolute necessity. You need to hunt for specific animals in order to make armor, and hunting is a simple timing minigame not unlike battling where you just have to wait for a cursor to line with with spots along a line. Click at the right time, and you catch the animal or fish you're going after.

While battles do yield money, grinding for cash is required because battles don't give enough. The minigame for hunting grows old very quickly, and the RNG based nature of it makes seeking specific animals a chore. Maybe you'll get the one you need right away. Maybe it'll take you multiple trips. It is very aggravating, to say the least. And by the end the battle system drags. It's fun for a bit, but the simple fact is that every single battle boils down to timing your button press properly and hoping your health outlasts the enemy's. Which, if you're keeping pace with armor, it will.

This is an incredibly ambitious title, propped up by a great presentation and a good enough narrative that evokes the likes of Lovecraft. - satisfying combat system
- difficult puzzles that really make you think
- interesting use of a hunting system
- most battles are challenging in an exciting way
Cons:
- no sell back to the blacksmith
- somewhat anti climatic final boss battle
- linear storyline but too little hints on what to do next
- gold is hard to come by and you can find yourself having to hunt/fish for a long period of time to make enough to properly equip yourself

Dark Fear is a brilliant combination of adventure, RPG and horror game elements.

(Note: Game completed offline, total play time was around 5-6 hours)

As an adventure game, the puzzles were a little on the easy side. But that's actually a plus because they were logical puzzles that can be solved with a bit of thought rather than heavily relying on guesswork or searching every screen for something you might have missed. Progress was at a steady pace and I was never stuck for an extended period of time.

The RPG elements work really well with the game. The protagonist can upgrade weapons and armor and buy items to gradually overcome stronger foes. It's also cleverly implemented: you can grind a little for money and supplies to make things easier, but you can't exactly abuse the system and become overpowered enough to break the game's sequence. There's a good amount of skill involved since you need to time your attacks to deal more damage and know when to use the right items. 

As for the horror aspect of the game, I'm very pleased with how the game sets the proper mood throughout different locations. The pixel art in the game has the right balance between looking retro yet polished enough for contemporary gaming. And the music is spot on for each area/event.

For those concerned, there are indeed jumpscares. Normally, I'd consider this the cheapest way to try making a game "scary" (involutary reflex actions vs. reactions from genuine fear). But surprisingly, I enjoyed them in this case. The game's dark, chilling atmosphere evokes a sense of dread, and it delivers each scare at an appropriate time.

All in all, a very enjoyable game.

Ein auf alt getrimmtes Abenteuer mit einem sich stetig wiederholenden Minispiel. Angesiedelt in einer mittelalterlichen, ländlichen Phantasieumgebung. 

Es gilt einige Dialoge zu führen und Gegenstände zu kombinieren. Dazu kommt eine Prise altbackene RPG-Mechanik: Es ist nötig seinen Charakter durch wertigere Ausrüstung zu verbessern. Die Mittel dafür erlangt man durch die Jagd auf diverse Tiere des Waldes. Das hört sich eventuell spannender an, als es ist. Dabei kommt das erwähnte Minispiel ins... Spiel. Ein Mauscursor fährt auf einer Leiste hin und her. Im richtigen Augenblick geklickt, bleibt der Cursor im Ziel stehen und etwa ein Angriff gilt als Erfolg. 
Dieser Mechanik ist der Spieler die ganze Zeit über ausgesetzt, beim Fangen von Wild oder beim Kampf gegen diverse Widersacher. Hin und wieder springt unter einigem Tamtam irgendein Vieh in's Bild und bedient damit den Horroraspekt.

Die Musik ist recht anhörlich und die Umgebungen sind stimmungsvoll gezeichnet.

Ohne die Geplänkel und die Ausrüsterei wäre wohl weniger Spiel übrig, die Erfahrung dafür konzentrierter. Wer Geduld für diese Art von Beschäftigungstherapie mitbringt und ein klein wenig Gruselstimmung sucht, kann sich in Dark Fear mal umsehen. 
Mir persönlich ist nach kurzer Zeit der Elan zum Weiterspielen verlorengegangen. Die Geschichte konnte mich nicht in ihren Bann ziehen. Darum wollte ich mir die, zum Vorankommen leider notwendige, Minispiel-Schufterei nicht mehr antun.
